name: Turmeric toothpaste

lead: Turmeric toothpaste is a paste containing turmeric, homemade or commercial, used as a natural whitener and for gum care. People are drawn to it as an additive-free option for brighter teeth.

Proponents point to anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties. Turmeric gets its colour from curcumin, a food colouring and historical dye, and reference sources report no high-quality evidence of health benefits for turmeric generally. No clinical studies of it for whitening were found.

paras: People brush with a turmeric paste, either bought or mixed at home with a base such as coconut oil or baking soda, in place of or alongside regular toothpaste. It is used daily or a few times a week, and results are described over weeks.
Turmeric is a strong yellow dye and colours materials, including cloth, sinks and potentially teeth and dental work if left on. No toothpaste-specific harm data were found.

angle.text: Users brush with turmeric paste as a natural whitener and gum-care option, even though turmeric is a strong yellow pigment. It is a homemade or store-bought alternative to conventional toothpaste. No trials of it for whitening were found.

lead: Turmeric toothpaste is a homemade paste or commercial toothpaste containing turmeric powder, used as a natural way to brighten teeth and freshen the mouth. It is part of the wider set of natural-whitening routines, alongside baking soda and oil pulling, that people try as an alternative to peroxide products. Homemade versions are typically powder mixed with coconut oil or baking soda, and the practice is sometimes called haldi tooth powder.

Proponents say turmeric's anti-inflammatory and antibacterial reputation helps clean teeth and soothe gums, and the spice has a long history in Ayurveda and other traditional systems.[1] The idea is counterintuitive, since turmeric gets its golden-yellow colour from curcumin and has historically been used as a dye and food colouring (E100); Wikipedia notes it makes a poor fabric dye because it is not light fast.[1]

No clinical trials of turmeric toothpaste for whitening were found, and a PubMed search for curcumin or turmeric toothpaste returned no results. Established whitening, by comparison, relies on peroxide gels, strips and trays, while whitening toothpastes typically rely on abrasives and are described as giving about one or two shades with continued use.[2]

paras: Recipes commonly combine turmeric powder with coconut oil or baking soda. Wikipedia describes baking soda as low-abrasive and effective for stain removal, with no adverse effects reported in clinical studies so far, though it is not presented as a bleaching agent.[2] Wikipedia also describes oil pulling as an Ayurvedic practice of swishing coconut or olive oil, and gives no evidence that it whitens teeth.[2]
The European Medicines Agency, as summarised on Wikipedia, found insufficient evidence of efficacy for turmeric and allows only traditional-use oral forms for mild digestive complaints.[1]

Wikipedia lists tobacco, coffee, tea, red wine, curry and tomato sauces among causes of surface (extrinsic) stains.[2] Professional whitening uses carbamide or hydrogen peroxide; at-home strips, gels and trays are also described, and sensitivity is common with peroxide treatments.[2]
No studies found. Turmeric and curcumin have been studied in many trials for other conditions, which Wikipedia describes as mostly low quality and without good evidence of benefit.[1]

Turmeric is a staining pigment used in dyes, and turmeric paper turns reddish-brown in alkaline conditions.[1] High-bioavailability turmeric supplements have been linked to rare liver injury, which concerns ingestion rather than toothpaste.[1] No studies of toothpaste-specific risks were found.
Turmeric paste appears in natural-whitening tips shared in appearance communities. No community discussion was available to cite.
